items.title: Azeem Azhar is going back to fountain pens to protect his thinking from AI
items.idea: In a 20-item gift guide, Azhar says he has returned to handwriting because he uses AI so much: "handwriting is how I protect my thinking." He sometimes dips a bare nib in ink so he has to stop every 10-15 words and reread. His loop is paper first, then dictation into Wispr Flow (editing as he speaks), with Otter for plain transcription.
items.angle: Heavy AI users are deliberately adding friction back, which is a small signal for analog goods (premium stationery, vinyl, hi-fi). It is also a useful talking point on how people protect their own judgment.
items.tweetA: One of the most AI-forward writers alive now dips a fountain pen in ink so he's forced to stop every 15 words. When the power users start adding friction back in, that's a signal. Analog is becoming the luxury good of the AI era.
items.tweetB: Workflow of a top AI thinker in 2026: think on paper → dictate → only then touch the model. The bottleneck was never typing speed. It's the quality of the first thought. Tools that make you faster at the wrong step are a tax.

items.title: A flattening US real yield curve says the dollar's 5% rally is close to topping
items.idea: The DXY is up about 5% since mid-September but reversed sharply this week from near 20-month highs. Simon White's lead indicator, the US real yield curve, has started to flatten, and real rate differentials are giving the dollar less support. A Fed pivot forced by economic stress would add more downside.
items.angle: This conflicts with Ironsides, which calls a hawkish hike on Dec 9 all but locked in. If White is right, the market is front-running the cure for high prices, which favors gold, EM and non-US equities.
items.tweetA: Dollar +5% since September, 20-month highs, then a sharp reversal the same week the Fed is supposed to hike. The real curve is flattening. When the currency stops responding to hawkish news, the news is priced. $DXY $GLD $EEM
items.tweetB: Everyone is a dollar bull into a Fed hike. But a hike into slowing earnings is how you flatten the real curve, and a flat real curve is how dollar tops start. The hawks may be building the dollar bear case themselves.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Bloomberg Simon White
items.title: US dependence on foreign buying of US stocks makes the dollar an AI-trade derivative
items.idea: White says America's 'extraordinary dependence' on foreign equity inflows to fund its current account deficit leaves the dollar exposed if Wall Street sells off again. The financing channel is foreigners buying US stocks, mostly AI megacaps, not Treasuries.
items.angle: The S&P fell 11.6% from its peak and NVDA fell 47.5%, so the flow channel is already being tested. If the dollar falls alongside an AI drawdown, a long dollar position stops working as a hedge for long US tech.
items.tweetA: The US current account is now financed by foreigners buying US stocks, and that mostly means AI megacaps. So the dollar is effectively short-vol on $NVDA. Last time stocks and the dollar fell together, a lot of FX hedges stopped working.
items.tweetB: Question nobody in FX is asking: what happens to the current account financing when the AI trade has its second leg down? Equity inflows were the plug. A $8T selloff in 45 days is a funding event, not just a P&L event.

items.title: Marvin Liao: the West has been in a hybrid war since the 2010s and is losing by doing nothing
items.idea: Liao reviews the Across Latitudes trilogy, a geopolitical thriller about the silent hybrid war between the West and Russia and Iran since the early 2010s. He says it went fully open with Ukraine and with Israel/US vs Iran. His claim is that he sees inaction at government, family and individual level, and that this is the Red Queen effect: 'inertia is death.'
items.angle: Pop culture is absorbing the 'permanent hybrid war' framing, which supports defense, cyber and resilience spending as long-lived secular themes rather than cycles.
items.tweetA: When geopolitical thrillers start reading like the newspaper, the market's 'peace dividend' assumptions are fiction too. Defense and cyber budgets aren't a cycle anymore. They're a baseline. $ITA $CIBR
items.tweetB: "Deciding to do nothing is also an action." True for governments and truer for portfolios. Most Western allocators are still positioned for a world that ended in 2014.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / TS Lombard Grace Fan
items.title: Next chip-war move: cut off maintenance, spare parts and software for tools China already owns
items.idea: China stockpiled much of the lithography equipment Washington wanted to block before the restrictions hit. So the next round of US measures may target spare parts, software updates, engineering support and servicing, controlling whether the installed base can keep running. That pulls the Netherlands (ASML) and Japan (TEL) into direct confrontation with Beijing.
items.angle: Service revenue from China is the hidden risk for ASML, LRCX, AMAT and TEL, and it is high-margin, recurring income. A ban on maintenance would be a recurring-revenue shock, not a one-off cut to orders.
items.tweetA: Washington can't stop China owning the lithography tools. It already bought them. So now the target is the service contract. For $ASML $LRCX $AMAT, installed-base service is the highest-margin, most recurring revenue they have. That's what's on the table.
items.tweetB: Machines without maintenance degrade on a timeline. A servicing ban turns China's stockpile into a melting ice cube with a known half-life. Watch Beijing's answer: it won't be chips, it'll be gallium, germanium and rare earths.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / TS Lombard Grace Fan
items.title: China's response to new chip curbs would come through critical minerals, and it is nearing a political window
items.idea: TS Lombard's 'Chip War Inflection Point' says the fight over AI computing capacity is nearing a critical political window. It argues Beijing's leverage, mainly critical minerals and the industrial supply chains that depend on them, could push the consequences well beyond semiconductors into broader markets.
items.angle: Escalation risk favors non-China rare earth and minor-metal suppliers (MP, Lynas) and pressures Japanese and Dutch exporters. It is a tail risk for the AI capex supply chain at the moment AI equities are most fragile.
items.tweetA: The chip war has been US move, China absorbs. The next round flips it: Beijing has spent years stockpiling tools and building mineral leverage. Asymmetric retaliation through rare earths is the scenario nobody's hedging. $MP $LYC
items.tweetB: The Netherlands and Japan are being asked to choose between Washington's export rules and Beijing's mineral supply. Europe's industrial base can't afford the second one. That's the pressure point to watch.

items.title: Ironsides: Trump's intervention in the Jensen affair fixed nothing, and the Fed hikes on Dec 9
items.idea: The S&P bounced 400 points, but the President's intervention in the Nvidia/Huang affair gapped stocks higher before most investors could trade. Ironsides says it lowered the odds of a disorderly AI credit event but did not answer the question of returns on AI capex now that capex growth has peaked. Hot capex, consumption and inflation data plus new tariffs make a hawkish hike on Dec 9 'all but locked in.' Corrections so far: S&P -12%, Tech -25%, SOX -43%.
items.angle: Ironsides is positioned for a hike into slowing earnings, which is the opposite of the 'dovish hike' consensus and the dollar-top call. Fading this bounce is the trade it implies.
items.tweetA: A presidential bailout of a CEO gapped the market up 400 points before anyone could trade it. That's not price discovery, it's a rescue. The capex-growth peak didn't get un-peaked. $SPY $SMH
items.tweetB: SOX -43%, Tech -25%, S&P -12%, and the Fed is about to HIKE. When was the last time the Fed tightened into a 40% semis drawdown? The 'Fed put' is either gone or it's coming in a much worse place.

items.title: Big Four AI capex hit 100% of cash flow in 1Q26, and from then on the cycle was rate-sensitive
items.idea: Ironsides' key claim: once the Big Four AI spenders' capex reached 100% of operating cash flow in 1Q26, their cost of capital rose sharply. That ended the argument that the AI investment cycle is insensitive to interest rates. They say that with real rates where they are, the valuation case for stocks 'rests on a flawed premise.'
items.angle: Ties to JPM's estimate (via AI Supremacy) that Big Tech cash flow covers less than 20% of $5.5T in AI buildout through 2030. The marginal dollar is now debt, so the Fed matters to MSFT, META, GOOGL and AMZN.
items.tweetA: Capex = 100% of cash flow. Past that line, every incremental GPU is funded with debt or equity, and the hyperscalers became rate-sensitive overnight. 'AI is immune to the Fed' died in 1Q26. Nobody updated the models. $MSFT $META $GOOGL $AMZN
items.tweetB: Combine two numbers: Big Four capex at 100% of cash flow, and JPM's estimate that internal cash covers less than 20% of the $5.5T buildout. The other 80% is bond market. The AI trade is a credit trade now.

items.title: Q3 GDP revised to 4.3% on capex while corporate income rises and worker income cools
items.idea: Q3 GDP was revised up to 4.3%, driven by corporate capex. Corporate income growth is surging while worker income growth is easing. Ironsides says the FOMC is 'driving with the rear-view mirror', focused on energy, tariffs and AI demand pushing prices up, while markets look ahead to weaker demand. New Section 301 tariffs due in late January add another demand shock. Even NY Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back hikes.
items.angle: A K-shaped income split plus a hike plus January tariffs points to consumer discretionary as the weak spot, while GDP prints stay strong because of capex. That is a recipe for a policy mistake.
items.tweetA: 4.3% GDP, and the composition is the story: capex surging, worker income cooling. Growth that comes from companies buying GPUs while paychecks slow isn't consumer strength. The Fed is hiking into the wrong half of the K. $XLY
items.tweetB: Williams, the Fed's resident dove, won't rule out consecutive hikes. If the doves sound like this, the 'dovish hike' crowd is going to have a rough December 9.

items.title: Helene Meisler: OIH has a possible head-and-shoulders bottom and is outperforming XLE
items.idea: Meisler's chart of the week is OIH, 'the one no one cares about anymore'. She sees a possible inverse head-and-shoulders bottom, and OIH outperformed XLE over the last week. She notes she always watches when the high-beta part of a group outperforms the low-beta part. XLE's head-and-shoulders top has not broken (yet).
items.angle: Oil services leading the majors is a classic early-cycle energy tell. Commodity Context and HFIR have been flagging tight balances, so this could be the equity market confirming it.
items.tweetA: Oil services: hated, under-owned, and quietly outperforming the majors for a week. High beta leading low beta is how sector turns start, not how they end. $OIH vs $XLE is the ratio I'm watching.
items.tweetB: XLE has a head-and-shoulders top that refuses to break. OIH has a head-and-shoulders bottom trying to form. When the same sector shows both patterns, the higher-beta one usually tells you which way it resolves. $OIH $SLB $HAL

items.title: TRIN printed 0.47 on Black Friday, its lowest since April 2025
items.idea: In Friday's holiday session, TRIN (the Arms Index) printed 0.47, the lowest since early April 2025. That is very strong buying breadth relative to volume. Meisler adds that the McClellan Summation Index has turned up, the junior Nasdaq (QQQJ) is still outperforming, and IWM gapped back above 270.
items.angle: April 2025 was the post-tariff-shock bottom. A comparable breadth thrust after an 11.6% S&P drawdown supports the bounce, which contradicts Ironsides' 'nothing is fixed' view.
items.tweetA: TRIN 0.47 on a half-day. Lowest since April 2025, which was THE bottom after the tariff shock. Breadth thrusts don't guarantee a bottom, but they rarely happen at the start of a bear leg. $SPY $IWM
items.tweetB: Macro guys: the Fed hikes into slowing earnings, nothing is fixed. Tape: lowest TRIN in 19 months, McClellan turning up, small caps gapping. Someone is very wrong into Dec 9.

items.title: 10-year yield set to retest the 5.00-5.15% zone, with insider selling 'done'
items.idea: Meisler asks whether the 10-year yield will test the 5.00-5.15% area again and points to a blue line to watch. She says insider selling looks done and asks whether insiders are buying. She also notes 'everyone is a dollar expert now', a contrarian read on DXY.
items.angle: A 10-year near 5% while the Fed hikes is a bear-flattener setup. If insider buying shows up into a 5% 10-year, that is a classic bottoming combination for equities.
items.tweetA: 10yr knocking on 5.00-5.15% for the second time while the Fed hikes. Double tops in yields at a hiking Fed are how bond bear markets end, not continue. $TLT
items.tweetB: 'Everyone is a dollar expert now' — Helene Meisler's sentiment read. Same weekend Simon White calls a dollar top on the real curve. Tape and macro are aligned on this one. $DXY

items.title: Sector tells: XBI crossed its downtrend, XLB never broke, INDA ignored, KWEB bounced into resistance
items.idea: Notes from Meisler's rounds: XBI had the chance to break down and didn't, and has now crossed its downtrend line. XLB 'never broke down', which she finds fascinating. ITA has two higher lows. ITB keeps basing. VGK filled its April gap. KWEB bounced into resistance. INDA has 'still no chatter.' She is adding CIBR to her watchlist.
items.angle: XBI breaking out while AI collapses would be a classic rotation, and biotech is the cleanest non-AI growth exposure. INDA with no chatter is the contrarian EM long.
items.tweetA: Biotech had every chance to break down during the AI liquidation and didn't. Now it's through the downtrend. When money leaves the crowded growth trade, it needs somewhere with no AI exposure to go. $XBI
items.tweetB: INDA: 'still no chatter.' India is the one big EM market nobody talks about while China gets a bounce-to-resistance. Quiet charts are where the next crowded trade comes from. $INDA $KWEB

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: Nvidia books the GPU sale today; CoreWeave carries the six-year depreciation bet
items.idea: Nvidia reported $115.8B in quarterly revenue and $77.5B in operating income, a ~67% operating margin. It recognizes revenue on delivery. CoreWeave depreciates the same GPUs over six years but must fund the purchase upfront. Q3: $3.66B revenue (+168%), $207M operating income, $846M net interest expense (over 4x operating income), $709M net loss. Debt principal is $47.5B against a $132.5B backlog.
items.angle: The profit sits at the center and the duration risk sits at the edge. CRWV interest coverage of about 0.24x is the stress indicator for neocloud credit, and it ties directly to the Fed hike debate.
items.tweetA: CoreWeave Q3: $207M operating income, $846M interest expense. Interest coverage of 0.24x. A Fed hike on Dec 9 doesn't hit $NVDA's 67% margin. It hits the companies that borrowed to buy the chips. $CRWV
items.tweetB: Nvidia books revenue the day the GPU ships. The buyer depreciates it over six years and pays interest the whole time. One company's income statement is another's six-year bet. That gap is the whole AI credit story. $NVDA $CRWV

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: Altman: AI demand has been 'double-counted', and most of the increase comes from two buyers
items.idea: According to materials from an Oct 31 Samsung meeting, Altman said parts of the market double-counted demand, especially for memory and data centers. By his count the big demand increase comes from just two companies, OpenAI and Anthropic. Every supplier plans to sell to the same few buyers, who won't buy from all of them. Microsoft RPO is $677B, Oracle ~$664B, CoreWeave backlog $132.5B.
items.angle: Memory (MU, Samsung, SK Hynix) is the most exposed to double-counted orders. Summed RPO is at least $1.47T against two customers whose Q3 revenue (Anthropic $17B) is a small fraction of it.
items.tweetA: $677B MSFT RPO + $664B ORCL + $132B CRWV = $1.47T in backlog. Altman says most new demand comes from TWO customers. Anthropic did $17B in Q3. When the buyer says demand is double-counted, believe the buyer. $MU $ORCL
items.tweetB: The most bearish AI quote of the year came from the biggest AI buyer: suppliers are all planning to sell to the same two customers. Memory is where double-ordering hits first, because memory always over-builds. $MU $SKHYNIX

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: Anthropic's IPO prospectus lists $900.9B in committed future spending
items.idea: Anthropic priced at $83, opened at $111.50 (+34%) and briefly traded near a $2T valuation, with $17B in Q3 revenue. The prospectus lists $900.9B in aggregate committed future spending, substantially all compute and infrastructure. Seven suppliers (Nvidia, Google, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, TSMC) bought $26B of shares in a private placement tied to the IPO. Amazon marks its $8B in convertible notes at ~$146.2B.
items.angle: $900.9B in commitments against a ~$68B annualized revenue run rate is about 13x, the AI version of an off-balance-sheet lease book. The supplier placement is circular financing in public-market form.
items.tweetA: Anthropic: $17B quarterly revenue, $900.9B in committed future spending. That's ~13 years of current revenue already promised to suppliers. And 7 of those suppliers bought $26B of the IPO. $ANT
items.tweetB: Amazon turned $8B of Anthropic notes into a ~$146B mark, while selling Anthropic the compute that justifies the valuation. Best trade of the decade or the cleanest example of circularity ever filed with the SEC? Probably both. $AMZN

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: Core Scientific gets 93% of its revenue from CoreWeave, funded with 7.75% secured notes
items.idea: Core Scientific, a former crypto miner, gets 93% of quarterly revenue from CoreWeave. In May it raised $3.3B in 7.75% senior secured notes. Its 590MW commitment is only ~13% of CoreWeave's 4.6GW+ contracted power, and only 485MW was billing at Sep 30. The 10% customer disclosure rule means the dependence is visible only from the smaller company's side: Microsoft and Nvidia don't name CoreWeave.
items.angle: There is a credit chain here: Core Scientific → CoreWeave → OpenAI/MSFT. The weakest link sits furthest from the profit. CORZ bonds are a way to express the neocloud credit view.
items.tweetA: Core Scientific: 93% of revenue from one customer, 7.75% secured debt, 105MW not yet billing. The customer is CoreWeave, which has 0.24x interest coverage. This is what the far edge of the AI spiral looks like. $CORZ $CRWV
items.tweetB: Disclosure asymmetry: Core Scientific must tell you CoreWeave is 93% of its revenue. Microsoft never has to tell you what it spends with CoreWeave. In AI, the public can only see the dependency from the side carrying the risk.

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: Nvidia as a lender: $105B in guarantees, $106B in equity stakes, a $500B financing platform
items.idea: Nvidia holds ~$61.7B in private equity investments and $44.2B in marketable securities. It agreed to guarantees capped at $105B for SB Energy's PORTS-Pike campus in Ohio, which leases to OpenAI. It partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman and KKR to mobilize $500B+ in third-party capital. Fed Governor Barr counts $100B+ in cumulative equity investment by chipmakers and hyperscalers into AI developers and clouds.
items.angle: Nvidia's contingent liabilities ($105B in guarantees alone) are close to a year of its operating income. That matters for credit spreads and governance, especially with an SEC accounting inquiry live.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's guarantee on ONE Ohio data center is capped at $105B. That's more than a year of operating income, contingent on OpenAI filling it. With an SEC accounting inquiry open, contingent liabilities are the line item I'd read first. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The supplier is now the bank, the guarantor, the equity investor and the capacity backstop. When the seller finances the demand, revenue quality is a credit question, not a growth question.

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: ComEd supply price up 53% in two years, with data centers a major driver
items.idea: Illinois consumer advocates report that ComEd's October 2026 electricity supply price was 53% higher than two years earlier, with data-center demand a major factor. ComEd has $3.1B in anticipated grid costs tied to 30 projects that ratepayers could inherit if projects fall through. JLL: data-center construction averages $11.3M/MW in 2026, plus up to $25M/MW for AI fit-out.
items.angle: Power prices are the political transmission channel for AI and drive state-level regulatory backlash (PJM, ERCOT, ComEd). At ~$36M/MW all-in, a 1GW campus costs ~$36B, which shows how much is at stake if demand moves.
items.tweetA: ComEd electricity supply +53% in two years. $3.1B in grid costs for data centers that may never get built. AI's first mass-market product isn't a chatbot. It's a higher utility bill. That's the voter-facing number. $EXC
items.tweetB: JLL: $11.3M/MW to build + up to $25M/MW to fit out = ~$36B per gigawatt. Demand can move between providers. The concrete and the substation can't. Stranded-asset risk lands on ratepayers first.

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: 121,000 US job cuts blamed on AI so far this year, while the RBA finds most firms' headcount unchanged
items.idea: Challenger counted 121,000+ US job cuts through October where the employer cited AI, more than twice last year's full-year total. The Reserve Bank of Australia's liaison survey found ~35% of businesses saw no productivity gain from AI and 30% only minor gains, with headcount unchanged by AI at about three in four firms.
items.angle: 'AI' is turning into a layoff narrative more than a cause. The productivity data (RBA) contradicts the layoff announcements (Challenger), which matters for the earnings quality of 'AI efficiency' stories.
items.tweetA: 121K US layoffs blamed on AI this year, double all of last year. Meanwhile the RBA finds 3 in 4 firms haven't changed headcount because of AI, and 65% see little or no productivity gain. 'AI' is the new 'restructuring.' It's a press release, not a productivity number.
items.tweetB: If 65% of firms report no or minor AI productivity gains, the AI-driven layoffs are a margin trade dressed up as a tech trade. That works until revenue needs the people you fired.

items.source: AI Supremacy / Andi Roach (The Complex Rebel)
items.title: Fed Financial Stability Report: hyperscaler and chipmaker debt sits in pension funds and insurers
items.idea: The Fed's November FSR flags rapid growth in AI-related borrowing, circular financing networks and complex obligations as possible sources of instability. It places most hyperscaler and chipmaker debt with mutual funds, pension funds and insurers. Addendum: JPM estimates the AI buildout needs $5.5T through 2030, and Big Tech's own cash flow covers under 20%. Margin debt is cited at $1.5T in 2026.
items.angle: AI capex is now a duration and credit risk held by the IG bond buyer base. Insurers' and pensions' exposure links an AI drawdown to life insurer spreads and private credit marks.
items.tweetA: JPM: $5.5T AI buildout through 2030, Big Tech cash covers less than 20%. The Fed: most of that debt sits in pensions and insurers. Your retirement account is a lender to the AI buildout whether you chose it or not. $LQD
items.tweetB: The Fed's own stability report now names 'circular financing networks.' When the regulator adopts the bears' vocabulary, the next step is disclosure rules. Watch for it.

items.title: Nvidia reinstated Huang after Trump pressed for it; stock +31%, then -5.9% on his 'terrible mistakes' remarks
items.idea: Nvidia's board brought Jensen Huang back as CEO and president on Monday after President Trump pressed for the move. Shares closed at $165.05, up 31%+. At his first all-hands back he admitted 'some terrible mistakes', said he violated the code of conduct and is in therapy, and the stock fell 5.9%. He faces several congressional probes and testifies at a Senate hearing on Dec 3.
items.angle: Dec 3 Senate testimony is the next binary catalyst, before the Dec 9 FOMC. Governance risk is now a priced factor in the largest index weight.
items.tweetA: $NVDA: +31% on a reinstatement the President pushed for, -5.9% when the CEO admitted he broke the code of conduct. Dec 3 Senate testimony, Dec 9 FOMC. The index's biggest weight now trades on governance headlines. Size accordingly.
items.tweetB: The playbook for founder-led mega caps just changed: the board fired the founder, and the White House un-fired him. Key-person risk is now political risk.

items.title: The AI selloff erased about $8T in 45 days, and NVDA fell 47.5% while growing revenue 103%
items.idea: The S&P 500 closed Nov 20 down 11.6% from its Oct 6 record. Nvidia fell 47.5% from its peak in the same weeks it reported 103% revenue growth. Anthropic closed 6.4% above its $83 IPO price. AI took 82.7% of US venture dollars through Q3 2026, so 2027 rounds will price against these marks.
items.angle: If revenue doubled and the stock halved, the multiple compressed about 4x. This is a discount-rate and governance crash, not a demand crash, which also explains why Anthropic held its IPO price.
items.tweetA: Nvidia: revenue +103%, stock -47.5%. Do the math: the multiple got cut by ~4x in weeks. That's not a demand problem. It's a discount-rate, governance and circularity problem, and only one of those can be fixed by earnings. $NVDA
items.tweetB: AI = 82.7% of US venture dollars through Q3. Public AI just lost $8T. Every 2027 private round now prices against public marks, so the down-round wave in AI startups hasn't started yet.

items.title: DeepMind: effective compute grows at least 10x a year, and METR's agent task length doubles every 88.6 days
items.idea: DeepMind's model puts algorithmic progress at 3-6x a year and investment growth at 2.5x, so effective compute grows at least 10x a year once faster chips are added. METR now measures agent task length doubling every 88.6 days: from 1-hour to 17-hour software tasks in 13 months.
items.angle: The capability curve keeps steepening while the financing curve breaks. Algorithmic gains of 3-6x a year mean less hardware per unit of capability, which is bearish for GPU unit demand if algorithms carry more of the load.
items.tweetA: METR: agent task length doubling every 88.6 days. 1-hour tasks to 17-hour tasks in 13 months. At that pace, a 1-week autonomous task arrives in under a year. The market is pricing an AI bust in the same quarter capability is accelerating.
items.tweetB: DeepMind's own math: algorithms improve 3-6x a year, hardware investment 2.5x. If software does more of the compounding than silicon, that's great for AI and awkward for the companies selling the silicon. $NVDA

items.title: Gumloop passes token costs through at cost plus an 8% fee: price -70%, trial conversion +42%
items.idea: Gumloop now passes token and compute costs through at cost and adds an 8% orchestration fee, close to OpenRouter's 5.5-8% take rates. The switch cut price per credit by 70% and lifted Pro trial conversion 42%. Separately, Emergence (560+ companies) finds 36% have cut SDRs, and ICONIQ finds AI-forward GTM teams are 20-43% smaller at the same ARR.
items.angle: AI app-layer pricing is converging on payments-style take rates (5-8%), which compresses SaaS gross margins toward marketplace economics. That is bearish for seat-based SaaS multiples (CRM, HUBS spend 33.9% and 43.6% of revenue on S&M).
items.tweetA: AI apps are converging on a 5-8% take rate on tokens. That's not SaaS pricing, that's Visa pricing. If software becomes a toll on compute, seat-based multiples are the wrong comp. $CRM $HUBS
items.tweetB: Gumloop cut prices 70% and conversion went UP 42%. Users want to see the meter. Transparency beats margin when the underlying cost falls 10x a year. Every AI company hiding token costs in 'credits' is on borrowed time.

items.title: Seed valuations are survivorship bias: Carta's $24M median only counts companies that closed
items.idea: Carta's median seed post-money rose to $24M at end-2025 from $18M a year earlier, but only companies that closed are counted. New seed deals price at ~4x the average and 10x the median active seed startup. ICONIQ: median AI-forward companies under $10M ARR grow 900% a year (4.5x T2D3 pace) with 55% gross margins and 105% NRR; the gap closes to 115% vs 100% above $100M ARR.
items.angle: 55% gross margins at the sub-$10M stage mean AI startups are buying growth with compute costs. Combined with the $8T public drawdown, 2027 seed and Series A pricing should compress.
items.tweetA: AI startups under $10M ARR: 900% growth, 55% gross margins. That's not software economics, it's reselling compute with a UI. Growth is buying the round, and the public market just repriced what growth is worth.
items.tweetB: Carta's median seed of $24M only counts survivors. New deals price at 10x the median active seed startup. The real median seed company isn't raising at all. It's quietly dying.

items.title: FCC clears SpaceX's 1-million-satellite 'Starmind' AI compute constellation
items.idea: The FCC authorized SpaceX's Starmind constellation of solar-powered AI computing satellites, and Chairman Carr said rival constellations will extend America's AI lead. Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society opposed it. Earthjustice says the approval skipped required environmental review.
items.angle: Orbital compute is now a regulatory reality. It is a long-dated threat to terrestrial data-center power economics (see ComEd +53%) and a valuation lever for the SpaceX/Tesla complex. Expect a legal challenge on NEPA.
items.tweetA: Same week: ComEd power prices +53% on data centers, and the FCC approves 1 MILLION solar-powered AI satellites. The grid problem is pushing compute off the planet. SpaceX just got a regulatory moat measured in orbital slots.
items.tweetB: Earthjustice says the FCC skipped the environmental review federal law requires for 1M satellites. Litigation is the real timeline here, not launch cadence. Amazon opposed it for a reason: Kuiper just lost the orbital land grab.

items.title: Notable's Anthropic bet is ~15x; GIC paid $4.5B+ for about 1%
items.idea: Notable Capital put ~10% of its US fund into Anthropic's Series E at a $61.5B valuation, now ~15x after the IPO at ~$1.5T fully diluted. GIC invested $4.5B+ across three rounds for ~1%; Baillie Gifford put in $1.5B. New funds: Kaszek VII $650M (LatAm), Kindred V $500M, Key1 $320M first close (95% returning LPs), Eleven Ventures €57M, CommerzVentures IV €50M, Iliad $33.4M MENA.
items.angle: One position returning 1.5x the whole fund is power-law concentration. LP DPI from the Anthropic IPO is a source of re-up liquidity for 2027 venture, partly offsetting the public AI drawdown.
items.tweetA: Notable put 10% of a fund into Anthropic at $61.5B. It's now ~15x, so that one check returns ~1.5x the entire fund. Venture isn't a portfolio business. It's a single-decision business with a portfolio attached.
items.tweetB: GIC: $4.5B+ for ~1% of Anthropic. Sovereign wealth is now the marginal late-stage AI buyer. When Singapore is your cap table anchor, AI is a state-capital asset class.

items.title: Anthropic moved its Messages API from Python to Rust and cut CPU per request 70%
items.idea: Anthropic rewrote its Messages API in Rust, cutting CPU per request ~70% and median time to first token ~20%, with no downtime and feature work continuing. Shadow traffic plus Claude agents took output parity from ~25% of inputs matching in April to public traffic on Rust by September. It also launched Claude Ship (Code Review GA, plus PR Steward and Claude Approvals betas) for Team/Enterprise on GitHub.
items.angle: AI agents doing large legacy rewrites is a real-world proof point, and it threatens IT services (ACN, INFY, EPAM) and the modernization-consulting business.
items.tweetA: Anthropic used its own agents to rewrite a production API from Python to Rust in ~5 months: CPU -70%, TTFT -20%, zero downtime. That is the $100B 'legacy modernization' consulting market, done in-house. $ACN $EPAM $INFY
items.tweetB: 70% less CPU per request is the boring AI story nobody prices: inference cost falls from software, not just chips. Every lab doing this cuts its own GPU demand at the margin.

items.title: GPT-6.2 designed protein minibinders: 35 of 322 bound their lab targets
items.idea: An internal OpenAI research model (GPT-6.2) matched or beat specialized biology models on many of 14 protein tasks using general reasoning and code. In wet-lab tests with Onava, 10.9% of its minibinder designs (35/322) bound targets across five targets, with specialized models still helping pick sequences.
items.angle: General-purpose models are encroaching on specialized bio-AI. That is a competitive threat to AI-drug-discovery pure plays and a tailwind for CROs and wet-lab capacity (the bottleneck moves to validation).
items.tweetA: A general-purpose LLM designed proteins with a 10.9% wet-lab hit rate. Specialized bio-AI startups raised billions on the premise that biology needs bespoke models. That premise just got a lot weaker. $RXRX
items.tweetB: If design is cheap and hit rates are ~11%, the bottleneck moves to the wet lab. The picks-and-shovels play in AI bio might be assay capacity, not models. $TMO $DHR

items.title: The UK's EDITH trial: AI replaces one of two mammogram readers for ~700,000 women
items.idea: The UK launched the world's largest AI breast cancer screening trial, inviting nearly 700,000 women across 30 sites. AI replaces one of the two human mammogram readers to test earlier detection and lighter radiologist workloads. The study costs roughly £10M, involves four AI companies and runs about three years.
items.angle: This is a template for AI substituting for a scarce clinical specialist under state-payer validation. Results are a reference case for reimbursement in the US and EU.
items.tweetA: The NHS is running a 700K-woman RCT on replacing half of radiologist reads with AI, for ~£10M. That's ~£14 per participant to potentially halve a specialist bottleneck. Single-payer systems will adopt AI faster than the US because they feel the labor shortage directly.
items.tweetB: AI in healthcare keeps being 'promising.' EDITH is different: 30 sites, 3 years, a regulator-grade answer. If it works, double-reading becomes single-reading plus AI everywhere.

items.title: Aaronson is 'virtually certain' AI labs hold crypto bombshells; RSA is still safe for now
items.idea: Scott Aaronson says he is 'virtually certain' AI labs hold cryptography bombshells, but the specific claim of fast factoring is an unconfirmed rumor. Google's Nov 25 factoring paper has big theoretical results but leaves today's RSA keys safe in practice.
items.angle: Post-quantum and post-AI cryptography migration is a slow-burn catalyst for cybersecurity spending (CIBR is on Meisler's watchlist) and a tail risk for crypto signature schemes (ECDSA).
items.tweetA: Scott Aaronson isn't a hype guy. When he says he's 'virtually certain' AI labs are sitting on cryptography bombshells, every bank, custodian and Bitcoin holder should be asking about their migration timeline. $BTC $CIBR
items.tweetB: Rumor: an AI lab broke RSA. Reality: no. But the market for 'crypto-agility' doesn't need the break, just the credible fear of one. Compliance budgets move on fear.

items.title: $7.6B+ is going into forward-deployed engineers; 7,300 US FDE postings in nine months
items.idea: Microsoft, AWS, OpenAI and Anthropic all launched forward-deployed engineer programs in 2026, with $7.6B+ committed and 7,300+ US job postings in the first nine months. ICONIQ: 62% of AI builders point FDEs at revenue or the product loop, 39% at implementation gaps. Atlassian's AI head says PM roles are growing fastest and Atlassian is hiring more juniors than ever.
items.angle: Labs are going Palantir-style, using services to capture enterprise adoption. That is evidence that AI value capture still needs humans in the loop, and a counterweight to the '121K AI layoffs' narrative.
items.tweetA: The labs selling 'AI replaces workers' are spending $7.6B to hire engineers who sit inside customers and make AI work. Adoption has a last mile, and it's staffed by humans. Palantir called this a decade ago. $PLTR
items.tweetB: 7,300 FDE job postings in 9 months. 36% of companies cut SDRs. AI isn't eliminating jobs evenly. It's moving headcount from selling software to implementing it.

items.title: Gemini 4 Neon wins a 25-task blind test; coding scores so close that cost and speed now decide
items.idea: In Lenny's Newsletter, six frontier models were scored blind across coding, writing, creative, video, prototyping and assistant tasks. Gemini 4 Neon won by a wide margin. Coding scores were so close that model choice comes down to cost and speed.
items.angle: Frontier commoditization in coding is a margin risk for labs and supports Google's distribution and TPU cost advantage, relevant to GOOGL vs a newly public Anthropic.
items.tweetA: Blind test, six frontier models: Gemini 4 Neon wins big, and coding is a statistical tie. When quality converges, the winner is whoever owns the cheapest compute. That's a TPU argument. $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Anthropic IPO'd at ~$1.5T the same month a blind benchmark called frontier coding a commodity. The moat is distribution and cost per token, not the model.

items.title: History: Nvidia had 30 days of cash in 1995 until Sega's $5M; Friendster turned down $30M of Google stock
items.idea: In 1995, after DirectX made triangles the PC standard, Nvidia's Sega chip project was scrapped and it was weeks from running out of cash. Huang asked Sega to convert a contract payment into a $5M equity investment, which funded the RIVA 128 (1997). Friendster turned down Google's $30M stock offer in 2003 (later worth ~$1B), lost its CEO in 2004 and lost to MySpace on 40-second page loads.
items.angle: Founder-control history is timely as Huang is reinstated by political pressure. It is useful context on how fragile category leaders are.
items.tweetA: Nvidia was 30 days from bankruptcy in 1995, saved by a $5M check from Sega. 31 years later, its CEO was saved by the President. Same man, two near-death experiences. Founder risk never goes away. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Friendster lost to MySpace because pages took 40 seconds to load. Not strategy, not funding: latency. Every AI app arguing about model quality should remember infrastructure decides who survives.

items.title: PDD: 15-20%+ FCF yield even after a 25% VIE haircut, and value heavyweights are buying
items.idea: The Hermit gives PDD a 9/10. Even after a 25% VIE discount, the business has a 15-20%+ free cash flow yield. Li Lu, Norbert Lou and Duan Yongping have all deployed large amounts of capital into the name in recent quarters. Their Pick of the Week basket is +15.87% equal-weighted since publication.
items.angle: PDD is a non-AI, cash-yield way into China consumer while KWEB bounces into resistance. Positioning by deep-value investors (Li Lu = Munger lineage) is the tell.
items.tweetA: Li Lu, Duan Yongping and Norbert Lou are all buying the same stock. It's not AI. It's $PDD at a 15-20% FCF yield after haircutting for the VIE. While the market liquidates AI at 40x, the value guys are buying cash flow at 5x.
items.tweetB: The AI trade just lost $8T. Meanwhile a company with a 15-20% FCF yield sits in the 'uninvestable' bucket. The cheapest assets in the world are the ones with a political discount, not a growth problem. $PDD

items.title: PDD's VIE share of revenue fell from 45.7% to 13.1% in two years
items.idea: The share of PDD revenue booked in the VIE dropped from 45.7% (2023) to 13.1% (2025) as activity moved to wholly owned subsidiaries and international entities (Temu via Whaleco). There are two separate regulatory risk buckets: onshore (SAMR, CAC, MIIT, VATS) for the PRC WFOEs and the VIE, and US/EU data privacy, customs/tariff and DSA exposure for the Temu entities.
items.angle: Structural de-risking of the VIE argues the 25% discount is too wide. But Temu's exposure to Section 301 tariffs (due late January, per Ironsides) and the EU DSA is now the bigger regulatory risk.
items.tweetA: PDD quietly moved its revenue out of the VIE: 45.7% → 13.1% in two years. The 'you only own a contract' discount assumes a structure the company has largely left behind. $PDD
items.tweetB: PDD traded VIE risk for tariff risk. Temu sits in Whaleco entities exposed to US customs, EU DSA and the new Section 301 tariffs due in late January. China risk didn't go away, it moved to Washington and Brussels.
